title: Africa’s green mineral partnerships: opportunity or trap?
body:
African countries are rapidly signing bilateral and multilateral green mineral partnerships with global actors to promote value addition. This surge reflects growing recognition of Africa’s strategic role in the global energy transition.

But design and governance matter.

These agreements are largely negotiated at the national level with individual African countries. Yet historical evidence suggests that unilateral mineral agreements with external actors have frequently resulted in extractive outcomes rather than durable development gains on the continent. Moreover, a recent policy report (https://lnkd.in/edc89ZJu) notes that while many of the nascent green mineral agreements include provisions on mineral value-chain integration, joint ventures, investment, knowledge transfer, and capacity building, most are negotiated with limited transparency, rely on vague and non-binding commitments, and have short time horizons.

What does this mean for Africa’s green mineral future?

- More agreements do not translate into structural transformation: The predominance of non-binding, time-limited, and opaque provisions in the design of these agreements limit their ability to induce durable investment in domestic processing and manufacturing. Without enforceable commitments and long-term horizons, these partnerships risk reproducing pit-to-port models under a green guise rather than enabling sustained industrial upgrading.
- Fragmentation kills scale and learning: While most of the green mineral agreements are negotiated at the national level, Africa’s true green industrialization strength lies at the regional level as we argued and showed in our recent report (https://lnkd.in/eJUPe8hF). It is thus safe to argue that Africa’s current approach to these agreements is self-sabotage.
- Uncertainty discourages long-term industrial investment: Vague commitments, limited transparency, and short validity periods create regulatory and policy uncertainty for both domestic and foreign investors. They discourage investments in smelting, refining, and intermediate manufacturing, activities that require patient capital, stable policy frameworks, and long-term demand certainty.

**Bottom line:** Africa’s green mineral future is not predetermined. Without stronger governance, regional coordination, and binding value-addition commitments, today’s “green partnerships” risk entrenching dependency. With strategic recalibration, they could underpin Africa’s green industrialization.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon Owusu Woubet Kassa, PhD
